title.rendered: Period Features ‘Sought After In Renovation Properties’

content.rendered:
New research has found that many Brits would be happy to take on a home that requires moderate to significant renovations, with people searching for a new home looking for a number of features.

Property Reporter shared the findings of the survey by Jackson-Stops, which revealed that over 80 per cent of people would be happy to buy a property that needed some work, with over 50 per cent of them willing to take on a major project.

When it comes to the things that people look for in a home, period features such as original fireplaces, were popular across all of the age groups surveyed. Another thing that prospective buyers look at is energy efficiency.

Among the 18 to 24 year old age group, a high-speed broadband connection was the most important factor determining whether they’d want to live in a given property.

Interestingly, 71 per cent of those questioned also said that they’d prefer to move to a larger home than extend their current property, a significant increase on the 59 per cent who said they’d prefer to move than improve in 2017.

Nick Leeming, chairman at Jackson-Stops, commented: “Many buyers enjoy the prospect of purchasing an older property and putting their own stamp on it, even if it means they have to wait a few months or even years before they can enjoy their dream home or location.”

Last year, Property Wire shared advice about which period features you can renovate to give your home a lift and help improve its value. Among the suggestions were cast iron fireplaces and radiators, vintage wooden flooring and timber windows.

title.rendered: Work Begins On Ipswich’s Unitarian Meeting House

content.rendered:
One of the oldest chapels in the country is to undergo a £550,000 restoration, with help from Historic England covering most of the cost, according to the Ipswich Star.

The 18th century Unitarian Meeting House, certainly one of Ipswich’s most significant buildings, has been a place of worship for 320 years, since opening its doors in 1700. The current congregation will be moving to a nearby community centre for the next seven months while the building is restored, updated, and given increased usability for more events.

On the day work began on the restoration, Historic England confirmed it would be making a grant for £421,000 for the work. The church had already raised £20,000 of its own, as well as been awarded further grants, boosting the funds to £125,000.

The rising Dissenter population in Ipswich in the 18th century gave cause for the church to be founded, and is now a Grade 1 listed building, along with its neighbour, the Willis headquarters.

Historic England has been heavily involved in the development of the plans for the project, giving expert fundraising advice, and technical guidance.

The Unitarian Meeting House had been placed on the Heritage at Risk Register due to the poor condition of the building, from which it will be removed once repairs are completed.

Tony Calladine, regional director at Historic England in the East of England said: “We’re pleased to play our part in repairing this important building and protecting it for future generations to enjoy. It will be a wonderful achievement to see it removed from the Heritage at Risk Register.”

title.rendered: What Are Listed Buildings?

content.rendered:
There are some incredible buildings dotted around the UK, both old and new, and it’s important from a historical perspective that these structures are preserved for future generations… and this is why we have listed building status, to ensure the protection of any sites of particular architectural or historic interest.

The older the building in question, the more likely it is to achieve listed status. Generally speaking, according to Historic England (which is in charge of looking after sites all over the country), any buildings built before 1700 and which are close to their original condition will most likely be listed.

As are the majority of buildings built between 1700 and 1850. It’s after 1945 that more careful selection is required and sites that are under 30 years old wouldn’t usually be viewed as having special historic or architectural interest because they haven’t stood the test of time.

There are grade I and grade II listed buildings, with grade I sites of exceptional interest. Just 2.5 per cent of all listed buildings are classified as grade I, while grade II* sites are important buildings of more than special interest (5.8 per cent of all listed buildings). Grade II buildings, meanwhile, are those of special interest, making up 91.7 per cent of all listed buildings.

Homeowners are most likely to find themselves living in grade II listed buildings and it’s important that you know your responsibilities where the structure is concerned, particularly when it comes to making changes.

Listed buildings are afforded extra legal protection within the planning system because of their importance to the nation and you will likely find that there is more control over what changes you can make to both the interior and exterior of the building – which is something to think about before you purchase a home of this kind.

If any work you have in mind will affect the special architectural or historic interest of the house, you will need to apply for listed building consent. Get in touch with your local authority conservation officer to see if consent will be required for what you have in mind.

When applications are considered, your planning authority will look in particular at the desirability of preserving the building, as well as its features and setting – and you would be wise to think about this when planning any changes you want to make.

Also bear in mind at all times that any unauthorised work you carry out on site will be considered a criminal offence and you could be prosecuted as a result. Planning authorities can also insist that any work done without consent in place be reversed, which could prove very expensive.

title.rendered: What Would You Do To Create Your Forever Home?

content.rendered:
While the start of a new year is often associated with making changes, many people in the UK have decided that one thing they’re not going to change in 2020 is their address. In fact, a growing number of homeowners appear to be deciding to make the best of where they live now.

Property Reporter shared the findings of a survey by LV= General Insurance, which revealed that 86 per cent of homeowners in the UK have decided to make changes to their current abode rather than moving somewhere new.

This equates to around 15 million people. The most popular way in which they’re making their home their own is to redecorate it in their own style. Over half (58 per cent) of those questioned said that this is what they intend to do in 2020.

Refurbishing the kitchen was the next most-popular renovation project to take on this year, with 50 per cent stating they’d do this, while 39 per cent said they’d focus their efforts on landscaping the garden.

The other two projects that made the top five, with 24 per cent each, were extending the house and painting its exterior.

Managing director of LV= General Insurance Direct business Heather Smith commented: “When looking to buy a property, especially one where you intend to stay put, it’s important to consider which factors are most important to you.”

If it’s living somewhere with period features, for example, you might want to consider how you can make the most of these, such as by investing in metal polishing in London to bring certain features back to their best.

But what if you haven’t found your forever home yet? Don’t worry as the survey revealed that people buy their forever home at an average age of 41, although many people who have yet to find their forever home believe they won’t buy it until they’re 49.

The research also found that over half (53 per cent) of people already live in their forever home.

It also revealed that the most important factor in a forever home is the garden, with 39 per cent of people citing this feature, while the number of bedrooms was second on the list, followed by access to amenities.

The Irish Times recently shared the results of the 2019 Houzz & Home Renovation Trends Study, which found that energy efficiency and using green materials in renovations are among the top considerations for homeowners making alterations to their properties.

As a result, the news provider made a number of recommendations of things that people can do to make their homes more energy efficient.

At the top of the list is switching to energy-efficient light bulbs, which is a low-cost measure and one that will not only save you energy but also reduce your electricity bills.

Replacing old windows for ones that are more thermally efficient is another suggestion, as is making sure that your attic is properly insulated to prevent heat from escaping through the roof.

When you’re planning to upgrade the insulation in your property, make sure you know how your home has been constructed and what insulation is already in place to ensure you make the most appropriate and safe changes, the news provider advised.

title.rendered: The UK’s Five Most Desirable Property Types

content.rendered:
If you could live in any property type, what would your preference be? Do you dream of a classic Victorian terrace, or perhaps an Edwardian country house? London building contractors have the answers for you.

For a quarter of Brits, Georgian detached houses are the ones we desire most. The grandeur of the great Georgian cites means that this style is always popular, and for this reason, many places with large stocks of such buildings, like Edinburgh, Bath and Brighton, tend to attract London-style prices.

The elegant style home, with symmetry and grandeur at the heart of its design, won favour over more modern builds. The top spot was closely followed by Victorian and Tudor style homes. For most Britons though, this remains an aspirational dream, owning a Regency townhouse or a Robert Adam country pile is something only to be contemplated in their wildest fantasies.

It’s harder to find similar properties in places like Glasgow and Manchester, whose architecture reflects the fact that they boomed during the reign of Queen Victoria. During the Victorian period, 1837 and 1901, a Gothic revival took place within the world of architecture. Homes built during this time were designed asymmetrically, with pointed arches and elaborate patterns.

Tudor homes were built between 1485 and 1603. These homes have a very distinctive, recognisable black and white appearance. Classic homes from this era often feature exposed timber frames, thatched roofs and narrow windows.

Most Brits would still like to have more modern conveniences in their homes, walk in showers, and underfloor heating, as well as making sure their homes are eco-friendly and efficient.

title.rendered: Camden’s Koko Nightclub Damaged In Fire

content.rendered:
Music venue Koko, which once served as Camden Place Ballroom, has been seriously damaged after a fire broke out earlier this week (January 6th), with firefighters able to save most of the main building, although the roof has been severely affected.

According to New Civil Engineer, the 100-year-old music venue – which is a Grade II listed building – has been closed for refurbishment work since March last year and had been scheduled for completion this spring.

Restoration work had been ongoing to rebuild the large copper dome and reinforce internal structures, but now it seems that the main dome and a big part of the roof have both been destroyed. The plans were for the dome and the fly tower to be transformed into a private hire venue and a new bar.

Georgia Gould, leader of Camden Council, commented: “Heartbreaking watching the Camden Palace/Koko up in flames this evening, a building that holds so many memories and means so much to us in Camden.”

All sorts of big name bands have taken to the Koko stage to wow crowds, including The Rolling Stones, The Faces, Coldplay, Madonna, Elton John, Prince and My Chemical Romance, to name but a few – and it’s a real shame to hear about the damage that has been done to such an iconic site.

As you can see, refurbishment and renovation work does come with risks attached, so it’s important that you do due diligence and choose a company you know has the skills and experience in place to ensure the job is completed satisfactorily.

title.rendered: Brass And Mixed Metals ‘Top Interiors Trend’

content.rendered:
If you’re getting ready to embark on a renovation project in 2020, it certainly pays to see what’s hot in the world of interior design. One trend that’s expected to be big in the coming year is brass, as well as mixing metals in interior design.

That’s according to Amy Kartheiser, an interior designer based in Chicago, who was one of a number of experts to recently share her trend predictions for our homes in 2020 with SFGate.

Speaking to the publication, she said that mixing brass with other metals is one of the best options if you want to incorporate this material into your home.

“Mixing metals is a great way to ensure brass doesn’t feel dated in a few years’ time,” she asserted. It’s also fine to combine brass and other warm-toned metals with the likes of chrome and silver, which are typically considered to be cooler in terms of colour.

To make sure you’re on trend with your brass, you also want it to have a more matte finish than you might be used to, the publication added.

Meanwhile, an article for The Zoe Report suggested that if you’re going to introduce dark colours into your home, you should think carefully about how you accessorise the space.

Offsetting dark shades with pale tones, particularly whites, is a good option, so consider these for soft furnishings like curtains. But you can also use metals, such as brass and chrome, to add some pop to walls painted in dark colours. Think the addition of picture frames or light fittings.

title.rendered: The Advantages Of Having A Wet Room

content.rendered:
Wet rooms are an amazing way to add functionality and style to your home. As well as creating a modern sleek look, they can also reduce cleaning, maintenance, and potentially add value to your home. If you’re planning any kind of home or building restoration in 2020, do not neglect your bathroom!

A recent report showed that the bathroom market is showing a strong uptake for renovations and restorations in the coming year. If you’re considering making such a change to your home, here’s some advantages of a wet room.

A wet room, as the name suggests, is a room that can get wet. The floor is tiled, and the room totally waterproofed (‘tanked’), instead of having a conventional shower tray. The need for shower doors and glass screens becomes redundant, as the water drains away via the gently sloping floor.

Whether you like the contemporary aesthetics or the convenience of a wet room, it’s also quite liberating to shower in a wet room, away from the constraints of the shower cubicle.

The wet room is space saving, especially for smaller bathrooms. It can make much better use of the space, creating functional, and practical usable space, with fewer bulky fittings and fixtures.

Fewer fittings and features mean that it’s easier too clean. Shower trays and screens and all the associated frame work gather dirt and grime, so eliminating all that creates an easier space to clean.

A wet room with non-slip flooring means that it is safer for children and those requiring easier access to showers, such as wheelchair users, and those with disabilities.

The aesthetic value of the wet room creates a definite wow factor. The clean lines, and minimalist design make it a much more sophisticated and stylish look than a standard bathroom.

Due to the waterproofing of the entire room, a wet room is incredibly resistant to moisture damage and leaks, leading to improved durability and it will keep your bathroom looking newer for longer.

title.rendered: Do You Need Your Parquet Floor Restored?

content.rendered:
One of the most time-consuming parts of an old house to restore is the flooring.

Carpets, lino and veneer flooring can work well in different settings, but if you already have wood floors it is worth considering restoring them.

Wood floors are attractive, hygienic and don’t harbour dust mites. They also don’t necessarily cost more to restore than buying new flooring.

So why might you need your parquet floor restored?

  1. There are loose tiles

It is a good idea to get these seen to asap as they can present a hazard, and may get damaged.

  1. It needs sanding

Scratches over time mean that a floor will eventually need resanding.

  1. It needs polishing

While some people prefer oils and waxes, lacquer is often considered a better bet for a hardwearing finish.

  1. It has been damaged

Whether it is from scratches, incorrect care or just age, a floor restoration service can bring it up like new.

  1. There are gaps inbetween tiles

This can be remedied with a specific technique that involves using the sawdust from sanding to fill in gaps.

If you do decide to have your parquet floor restored then you need to consider bringing in the professionals. Laying parquet tiles is a tricky and time-consuming job.

More importantly, it is important to not attempt to sand your floors yourself using a standard drum sander. This is as parquet floors have the grain running in different directions and a drum sander doesn’t handle this well. You need a specific type of sander to deal with delicate parquet flooring.

title.rendered: Old House Restoration Tips

content.rendered:
Restoring an old house can be an incredibly rewarding project, providing you the satisfaction of living in your newly renovated home, or an opportunity to sell at a profit, but it can also be a daunting task.

If you’ve bought, or are considering buying, a fixer upper, you may be wondering how to start tackling such a large project. Here are our tips to get you started.

Before undertaking your project, have the house inspected to avoid any nasty surprises during renovation – it’s best to tackle any structural or mechanical issues, damp problems or roof repairs right from the get-go.

Once you’ve identified any problems, it’s important to prioritise your projects. It can be tempting to jump into the fun details like designing the kitchen and bathroom, but it is essential to tend to features that could potentially cause further damage first, such as the roof and windows.

Sustainability is the property trend that is here to stay, with homeowners citing it as a top priority. Make your home more attractive to buyers by improving energy and water efficiency. Even if you’re not planning to sell in the near future, you will reduce your electricity and water bills!

Recycling and upcycling are also excellent ways to sustainably renovate your home, and will add a modern twist to period houses. Salvaged timber and antique pieces are great places to start and will also save you money – the only limit is your imagination!

Many old fixtures can be brought back to their former glory with a little TLC, even if they’re past their best – just make sure to proceed with caution when cleaning them to avoid further damage. When in doubt, it’s best to consult a professional, particularly for tasks such as shot blasting and metal polishing.

A six-bedroom property that dates back to the early 20th Century located on Sauncey Avenue has gone on sale for £1.9 million.

Viewers will discover the property boasts an entrance hall, living room, dining area, utility room, family snug, cloakroom and large kitchen/breakfast space.

There is also a master bedroom with en suite and dressing room on the first floor, as well as three other bedrooms and one large family bathroom. Finally, the second floor has two more bedrooms, one with an en suite.

Among its desirable original features are wooden beams, timber flooring, a fireplace, and a Tudor-style façade.

When looking for a property, period features remains one of the most popular criteria for homebuyers. Indeed, a survey by discountflooringdepot.co.uk revealed original features was why more than half (51 per cent) of people prefer period properties to new-builds.

title.rendered: Peckham ‘Top Urban District’

content.rendered:
Peckham’s reputation has changed considerably in recent years. It’s gone from being one of the most deprived districts in London to one of its trendiest – and property prices are reflecting the shift.

That’s according to research published by Homes and Property, which has found that house price growth in Peckham has outpaced every other UK district since 1995 when records began. Knight Frank carried out the detailed analysis of Land Registry data, which showed prices here have grown by a staggering 1,082 per cent since 1995.

One of the reasons why Peckham has become such a popular hotspot is because many of its unusual buildings have been saved from demolition.

Eileen Conn is named as a key figure in this. She founded the group Peckham Vision, which rescued buildings and spaces in the area around Peckham Rye station. These all “contribute to Peckham’s special identity”, the news provider noted.

“Since 2005, the group have campaigned to highlight reuse and restoration. Existing buildings are a record of social and visual history – they affect the sense of place and identity of an area,” Ms Conn stated.

This goes to show the importance of restoring existing buildings, rather than just demolishing them to make way for new properties. Restoring buildings with care and love can have stunning results, as demonstrated in Peckham.

If you’ve been considering buying a period home, but haven’t taken the plunge yet, now could be the time to do it. Another article for Homes and Property noted that only new build homes have seen prices increase in every borough in the capital since 2014.

Since the referendum to leave the EU, prices of existing homes in the capital have declined by 2.1 per cent, whereas the cost of buying a new-build home has risen by 1.6 per cent in the same period.

title.rendered: UK’s Top 10 Most Endangered Buildings Revealed

content.rendered:
The top ten most endangered buildings around the UK has been revealed, compiled by the Victorian Society, with the director of the organisation describing it as a “particularly rich mix”.

The list included Shadwell Court in Norfolk, the Chatterley Whitfield Colliery in Staffordshire, Everton Library in Liverpool and Hulme Hippodrome in Manchester.

Society president Griff Rhys Jones explained that the list includes some real historical monuments and it makes for both “inspiring and saddening” reading, featuring theatres, pubs, libraries, Victorian mansions, schools and more.

“Can we really want to lose a sturdy industrial site like Chatterley Whitfield Colliery near Stoke? Or a fine school in Glamorgan or worthy industrial frontage in the now newly flourishing Jewellery Quarter in Birmingham?

“All of these historic sites are glorious and imaginative places ready for a new and productive life. How incredible that should feature on the Top Ten Endangered Buildings list. Let us hope that people spring into action and pay attention,” he went on to say.

The Corn Exchange in Swindon is also on the list, a ruined complex in the middle of the Old Town. Urgent action is now needed to save the building from further deterioration, with numerous redevelopment proposals having come and gone.

More buildings look set to be revitalised around the UK as well, thanks to a fresh wave of funding from the government to the tune of £95 million. The selected projects will be working alongside Historic England to develop plans to breathe new life into their high streets over a four-year programme.

title.rendered: How To Look After Original Wood Flooring

content.rendered:
Wood flooring can really bring a house to life, showing off a period property’s original features and helping to restore its antiquated look. Carpets can hide a house’s best fixtures, so stripping them back and showing off the original timber can highlight its period charm.

However, this is only if the flooring has been looked after well. Here are some tips on how to maintain your original floor so it can last several years more.

  • Regular maintenance

The trick to making sure wooden floorboards look good, even after decades, is to take care of them regularly. This includes wiping away spills immediately so no stains are allowed to soak into the wood. This also prevents water damage, such as warping, from occurring.

It is also important to sweep or vacuum the floor at least twice a week, according to Real Simple, to get rid of any dust and debris brought into the house. If left to accumulate, these will build up and cause a layer of dirt to form, which becomes harder to shift.

  • Protection

As well as keeping it clean, it is important to protect it from further damage. For instance, you should remove shoes – especially high heels – as these can create dents and scratches that are hard to get rid of.

You should also be careful when moving heavy furniture by picking them up instead of dragging. Having a rug in busy areas, such as hallways or in the lounge, is a good idea as well, as this will add further protection.

  • Restoring services

To really bring your floor back to life, it is a good idea to employ restoration services that can rejuvenate these period features.

By sanding a layer of wood, the top layer of dirt is removed, and any signs of wear and tear are gone for good.

title.rendered: Imperial Science Collage

content.rendered:
On this project, The Complete Restoration Company had many different substrates and surfaces to restore, each requiring their own very specific treatment.

Our versatile Doff machine was used to clean a number of surfaces – the hot water blasting treatment helped bring the Portland stone treads and risers back to their best, and its steam setting helped us clean and polish the glazed bricks in the foyer.

The terrazzo floors in reception were carefully cut back to their original finish and then re-polished.

Next to be restored were the bronze balustrades that lined the four flights of stairs. They hadn’t been cleaned for some time, but a good polish and re-lacquer soon made them look as good as new.

And finally, the top landings and flight of stairs had been finished in a parquet floor that had been neglected for years. The Complete Restoration Company re-fitted any loose blocks, sanded then polished them with three coats of a polytec hard wax oil.

title.rendered: Victorian Residence

content.rendered:
From oak floors to pine doors, The Complete Restoration Company undertook and managed the whole restoration process for this particular project.

Replacement period fireplaces were installed, whilst existing fireplaces were re-conditioned and made safe.

A new kitchen was designed and built by our master craftsman for a bespoke look that is in keeping with the style of the property. Bathrooms were updated and modernised leaving. clean modern feel which will last for years to come

The floorboards were removed and replaced with oak flooring that was distressed to give it an antique feel. After which a series of organic hard wax oils were used to seal and finish it. The period renovation even extended to the fully refurbished Victorian radiators, all of which were supplied and fitted to Corgi standards.

The original doors were long gone, but period doors were sourced, stripped of paint and finished with beeswax. The original sash windows were reconditioned on site, the sash cords were replaced and the wood was stripped back, primed and repainted in a colour that suited its surroundings. By the time The Complete Restoration Company left the building, it looked truly beautiful!

title.rendered: Halcyon Gallery

content.rendered:
The Halcyon Gallery has become known as one of Europe’s leading art galleries, representing some of the finest contemporary painters and sculptors.

It was no surprise that they requested The Complete Restoration Company to restore their breathtaking Georgian staircase back to a work of art.

All of the original features were completely covered with years and years of caked on paint, so it was necessary to restore the entire staircase in a considerate and fitting way.

The cantilevered staircase was stripped of paint using the environmentally friendly Doff Cleaning System, ensuring that only the paint was removed and the delicate limestone remained undamaged. We then honed back the limestone using diamond polishing pads and finally impregnated it with a limestone sealant.

The cast and wrought iron balustrades were sand blasted to remove ugly layers of paint and then polished to make the most of the original finish. Finally, the mahogany handrail was stripped and re-polished by our expert French Polishing team.

title.rendered: Haileybury College

content.rendered:
Originally built in 1806 as a training college for budding civil servants bound for India, Haileybury eventually became an independent school that taught luminaries including Clement Atlee, Sir Stirling Moss and Rudyard Kipling.

Being such an old school, maintenance and upkeep of its many original features have to be undertaken carefully and respectfully. This is one of the reasons that The Complete Restoration Company were asked to repair and polish their rather neglected 100-year-old Dining Hall floor.

Some of the original parquet flooring was carefully restored and re-fitted and doormat wells were made larger before a series of meticulous sanding processes brought the original wood back to its former glory. Finally, three coats of a polytec hard wax oil were applied to protect it from the thunder of hungry students’ feet.
